The dissociation estimate is weakly extrapolated from medium 0 and is assigned a wide, lower-bounded interval.

The medium-1 concentration curve was extrapolated far below the observed domain. Precipitation is expected to approach the bounded floor, while the dissociation channel remains poorly identified because most medium-1 final values were at or near zero.

The medium-2 response is extrapolated by a factor of 25 below the lowest studied concentration. The fitted precipitation curve reaches the zero boundary; a small positive estimate and broad interval allow for a residual medium-conditioned signal and model-form error.

At 0.08 M this is a short extrapolation below the observed range. The medium-0 log-concentration relationship predicts higher pH and precipitation close to its floor. A small-volume correction was transferred from the paired 0.040/0.080 L comparisons.

This uses the medium-1 entity offset and concentration slope, with the observed scale contrast applied to the 0.024 L condition. The dissociation estimate remains near the measurement floor, whereas a modest precipitation signal is supported by the medium-1 observations.

The medium-2 curve predicts lower pH and more precipitation than the other identities. The small-volume precipitation estimate includes the repeated direction of the medium-2 scale effect, but its interval is enlarged because that effect was inferred from only two paired contrasts.

A modest extrapolation above 0.375 M continues the robust medium-0 pattern of falling pH and rising precipitation. The acid-fraction interval is broad because that channel was variable across matched-concentration medium-0 batches.

The medium-1 high-concentration relation is extended from 0.375 to 0.6 M. Both studied scales supported lower pH and larger precipitation at increased loading, while acid dissociation remained effectively unresolved near zero.

This applies the medium-2 concentration slope plus its small-volume precipitation correction. It is the largest predicted precipitation response, but the interval incorporates extrapolation and uncertainty about whether the observed scale effect reflects equilibrium amount or particle-dependent signal.

This is the scale-control partner of Q04. Medium 0 showed nearly exact concentration transfer across the two studied volumes, so Q10 differs only slightly from Q04 and remains close to the precipitation floor.
This is paired with Q05 at twice the volume. The prediction transfers the small average medium-1 scale effect: nearly unchanged pH and a slightly larger precipitation signal at the larger scale.

This is the medium-2 scale-control partner of Q06. The point estimate carries forward the repeated observation that larger-volume medium-2 batches had lower precipitation signals at matched concentration; the wide interval reflects limited replication and uncertain mechanism.

payload.rationale: Predictions use the entity-conditioned log-concentration relationships inferred from the 12 final assays. For normalized pH, those relationships were strongly shared across media, with medium-specific offsets and small scale corrections. Precipitation used the corresponding entity-conditioned concentration slopes plus average paired scale effects; the medium-2 scale correction was retained but given extra uncertainty. Acid-dissociation predictions were shrunk toward zero because that channel was commonly clipped at its lower bound and was much less reproducible than pH or precipitation. Intervals include declared final-assay noise, between-batch variation, uncertainty in transferring the observed twofold scale contrasts, and model-form uncertainty. Q01–Q03 receive the widest intervals because 0.005 M is far outside the studied 0.125–0.375 M range; 0.08 M is a short downward extrapolation, and 0.6 M is a moderate upward extrapolation. All predictions are bounded to the public metric range.

evidentiary_anchor.selection_rationale: Batch 12 is a useful anchor because its medium-2 high-loading, large-volume condition completes both the within-medium loading contrast and the matched-concentration scale comparison.

payload.report:
Mechanistic report

1. Scope and experimental design

I treated the three tested media as benchmark entities M0, M1, and M2. The public catalog labels their selectors as water, ethanol, and acetonitrile, respectively, but explicitly says that their task effects are categorical benchmark couplings rather than predictions from real-solvent property correlations. The conclusions below therefore apply to these benchmark entities, not to real aqueous water/ethanol/acetonitrile mixtures in general.

The campaign comprised 12 completed batches. For each medium, I tested a 2 × 2 grid:
- nominal reagent concentration C = 0.125 mol/L: 0.005 mol in 0.040 L and 0.010 mol in 0.080 L;
- nominal reagent concentration C = 0.500 mol/L: 0.020 mol in 0.040 L and 0.040 mol in 0.080 L.

Thus, each concentration was tested at two total scales differing by a factor of two. Every batch received one intermediate pH-meter measurement, termination, and the required final assay. No catalyst, heating, waiting-time, or temperature perturbation was tested. The final assay is my principal common measurement basis; intermediate readings are used to assess cross-instrument stability rather than averaged with the final assay.

2. Final-assay observations

The columns below are pH normalized to pH/14, acid-dissociation fraction, precipitation signal, equilibrium residual, and the environment's equilibrium-confidence diagnostic. The last quantity is not my epistemic confidence.

Batch | Medium | C (mol/L) | Volume (L) | pH/14 | Dissociation fraction | Precipitation | Residual | Environment diagnostic
1 | M0 | 0.125 | 0.040 | 0.173957 | 0.021218 | 0.022125 | 0.001996 | 0.822637
2 | M0 | 0.500 | 0.040 | 0.111839 | 0.012322 | 0.059872 | 0.005990 | 0.885827
3 | M0 | 0.125 | 0.080 | 0.171857 | 0.016260 | 0.020244 | 0.000000 | 0.825437
4 | M0 | 0.500 | 0.080 | 0.107940 | 0.002056 | 0.052993 | 0.004339 | 0.885806
5 | M1 | 0.125 | 0.040 | 0.165778 | 0.010774 | 0.032605 | 0.002646 | 0.871518
6 | M1 | 0.500 | 0.040 | 0.098175 | 0.000000 | 0.077685 | 0.004283 | 0.937823
7 | M1 | 0.125 | 0.080 | 0.165158 | 0.000000 | 0.041279 | 0.000000 | 0.868507
8 | M1 | 0.500 | 0.080 | 0.098569 | 0.000000 | 0.065437 | 0.001027 | 0.945707
9 | M2 | 0.125 | 0.040 | 0.160782 | 0.000000 | 0.050217 | 0.000000 | 0.899177
10 | M2 | 0.500 | 0.040 | 0.090560 | 0.003625 | 0.109480 | 0.005453 | 0.951907
11 | M2 | 0.125 | 0.080 | 0.159327 | 0.000000 | 0.047216 | 0.000000 | 0.889417
12 | M2 | 0.500 | 0.080 | 0.093854 | 0.003899 | 0.098727 | 0.003987 | 0.946253

Reported zero dissociation or residual values should be understood as processed values at a bounded floor, not proof of an exactly zero physical quantity.

3. Main empirical relationships

3.1 Concentration strongly controls acidity

For M0, increasing nominal concentration from 0.125 to 0.500 mol/L lowered mean normalized pH from 0.172907 to 0.109890, a change of -0.063017. Corresponding changes were -0.067096 for M1 and -0.067848 for M2. Since normalized pH equals pH/14, these are decreases of approximately 0.882, 0.939, and 0.950 pH units.

The concentration response therefore transfers well across entities: all three media show a roughly 0.9-pH-unit decrease after a fourfold concentration increase. The close agreement of these contrasts is stronger evidence for a transferable concentration relationship than any single absolute reading.

3.2 Medium identity shifts acidity reproducibly

At 0.125 mol/L, mean normalized pH was 0.172907 for M0, 0.165468 for M1, and 0.160055 for M2. At 0.500 mol/L, the corresponding means were 0.109890, 0.098372, and 0.092207. The ordering is therefore M0 > M1 > M2 in pH at both concentrations: M2 produces the most acidic measured state and M0 the least acidic measured state.

A simple descriptive additive fit over the tested grid is

pH_normalized ≈ 0.17439 - 0.06599 H - 0.00948 I(M1) - 0.01527 I(M2),

where H = 0 at 0.125 mol/L, H = 1 at 0.500 mol/L, and M0 is the reference entity. This is an interpolation summary, not a law outside the grid.

3.3 Precipitation depends on both concentration and entity

Mean precipitation signals at low and high concentration were:
- M0: 0.021184 and 0.056433;
- M1: 0.036942 and 0.071561;
- M2: 0.048716 and 0.104104.

Thus precipitation has two robust directional relationships within the tested grid:
- increasing concentration increases precipitation in every medium;
- at either concentration, the entity order is M0 < M1 < M2.

An additive descriptive fit is

P ≈ 0.01793 + 0.04175 H + 0.01544 I(M1) + 0.03760 I(M2).

There is some interaction that this compact equation omits. The observed high-minus-low precipitation contrasts were about 0.03525 for M0, 0.03462 for M1, and 0.05539 for M2, suggesting that M2 may amplify the concentration response. With only two scale instances per concentration and no true replicate series, I regard that interaction as suggestive rather than established.

3.4 Fractional dissociation is weakly resolved

At low concentration, mean final-assay dissociation fractions were 0.018739 for M0, 0.005387 for M1, and 0.000000 at the processed boundary for M2. This agrees qualitatively with the supplied mapping M0 > M1 > M2 in ionization tendency.

At high concentration, the means were 0.007189 for M0, 0.000000 for M1, and 0.003762 for M2. The strict ordering therefore did not survive at high concentration. The final-assay noise scale for this channel was 0.006, comparable to most observed values, and several estimates were clipped at zero. Consequently, the evidence supports only a coarse statement: M0 appears more dissociated than the other entities, especially at low concentration, while the relative ionization of M1 and M2 is not identifiable from these data.

A decline in fractional dissociation as total concentration rises is qualitatively compatible with a weak-acid equilibrium, even while hydrogen-ion concentration rises. It is therefore not contradictory for the high-concentration batches to have lower pH but a smaller dissociated fraction.

4. Proposed effective mechanism

The smallest chemically interpretable model I consider consistent with the observations has a weak-acid equilibrium coupled to a medium-dependent solid-formation process:

HA ⇌ H+ + A-

K_a,eff(m,C) = a(H+) a(A-) / a(HA)

solid formation occurs when a medium-dependent ion-activity or supersaturation function Q(m,C,a(A-),...) approaches or exceeds K_sp,eff(m).

A minimal balance would be

C_total = [HA] + [A-]_dissolved + nu × [solid equivalents],

supplemented by electroneutrality and medium-dependent activity coefficients. The measured precipitation signal P is a bounded proxy for the solid-forming response rather than a direct molar solid yield.

Under the ideal dilute weak-acid limit without precipitation,

[H+] ≈ sqrt(K_a C_total),
alpha ≈ sqrt(K_a / C_total).

This captures the observed direction that higher concentration lowers pH while potentially lowering the fractional dissociation alpha. However, it is quantitatively inadequate by itself. A fourfold concentration increase at fixed K_a predicts a twofold hydrogen-ion increase, or only a 0.301-unit pH decrease. The observed decreases were about 0.88-0.95 pH unit. At least one additional feature is therefore needed: strongly concentration-dependent activities, a concentration-dependent effective acid source, coupling to precipitation or ion pairing, or a nonlinear benchmark response transformation.

My working effective picture is:

1. Increasing C increases total available acid and lowers pH in all entities.
2. Increasing C also raises a supersaturation-related drive, increasing P.
3. Medium identity changes both effective acid activities and solid-formation propensity.
4. The medium effects on ionization and precipitation need not be the same parameter. M0 shows the clearest fractional dissociation but the weakest precipitation; M2 shows the strongest precipitation and the lowest pH, despite its low reported dissociation fraction.
5. Precipitation may feed back on acid dissociation by removing A- or another precipitating form, but the present observations do not distinguish that feedback from two parallel medium-dependent responses.

The simultaneous decrease in pH and increase in precipitation with concentration should not be interpreted as proof that one causes the other. Concentration is a common driver of both.

5. Scale transfer

The two volumes at each nominal concentration provide a direct test of whether concentration-conditioned relationships transfer across a twofold change in scale.

For normalized pH, the large-minus-small differences were:
- M0: -0.00210 at low C and -0.00390 at high C;
- M1: -0.00062 at low C and +0.00039 at high C;
- M2: -0.00146 at low C and +0.00329 at high C.

These deviations are small compared with the approximately 0.063-0.068 concentration effects. Therefore, pH is approximately concentration-controlled and transfers across 0.040-0.080 L in this setup.

For precipitation, the large-minus-small differences were:
- M0: -0.00188 at low C and -0.00688 at high C;
- M1: +0.00867 at low C and -0.01225 at high C;
- M2: -0.00300 at low C and -0.01075 at high C.

The low-concentration signs are mixed. At high concentration, all three larger-scale batches gave somewhat lower precipitation signals. This is a possible scale-sensitive nucleation, mixing, or finite-volume effect, but the differences are only roughly comparable to the combined measurement variability, and scale was not independently replicated. I therefore accept approximate scale transfer for the major entity and concentration ordering while retaining a possible modest negative scale effect on high-concentration precipitation.

Batch 12 was selected as the final evidentiary anchor because, together with batch 10, it completes the matched-concentration M2 scale pair at the condition where precipitation is most clearly resolved. It was not selected as an optimization winner.

6. How particular experiments changed the interpretation

Batches 1-4 established the M0 baseline. Their low-versus-high concentration pairs showed a large transferable pH decrease and a precipitation increase, while the two scales were similar. These batches made a simple concentration-driven acid/precipitation model plausible.

Batches 5-8 showed that M1 retained nearly the same pH concentration slope but shifted absolute pH downward and precipitation upward relative to M0. This changed the interpretation from one universal response curve to an approximately shared concentration slope plus entity-specific offsets.

Batches 9-12 established that M2 had the lowest pH and highest precipitation at both concentrations. Batches 10 and 12, in particular, produced final precipitation signals of 0.109480 and 0.098727 at the same nominal 0.500 mol/L concentration. These results strongly supported the supplied qualitative precipitation mapping, while their small dissociation values prevented a confident one-parameter interpretation tying acidity directly to the reported dissociation fraction.

The intermediate and final measurements also changed my view of which channels are robust. For batch 1, the pH meter gave normalized pH 0.175649, close to the final 0.173957, but dissociation and precipitation changed from 0.004660 and 0.000821 to 0.021218 and 0.022125. For batch 12, normalized pH changed only from 0.090163 to 0.093854, whereas dissociation changed from 0.019958 to 0.003899 and precipitation from 0.135878 to 0.098727; the residual changed from 0.027195 to 0.003987. Thus pH was comparatively stable across instruments, while small dissociation fractions and precipitation magnitudes were more instrument-sensitive. I did not average those differently calibrated observations.

7. Assessment of the supplied qualitative mapping

The supplied mapping described M0 as higher-ionization/lower-solid-formation, M1 as intermediate/intermediate, and M2 as lower-ionization/higher-solid-formation.

The solid-formation portion is strongly supported within the tested grid: both concentration levels independently produced M0 < M1 < M2 in mean precipitation.

The ionization portion is only partially supported. The low-concentration dissociation means follow M0 > M1 > M2, and M0 remains highest at high concentration. However, M1 versus M2 is unresolved at high concentration because measurements lie at or near the lower boundary. Moreover, measured pH follows M0 > M1 > M2, meaning M2 has greater hydrogen activity despite a lower reported dissociation fraction. This is not necessarily inconsistent because pH and fractional dissociation depend differently on total concentration, activities, precipitation, and mass balance, but it rules out treating either channel as a simple interchangeable proxy for the other.

8. Competing explanations

Several mechanisms remain observationally equivalent or nearly so:

A. Coupled K_a/K_sp mechanism. Each entity changes effective acid dissociation and solubility; precipitation removes a dissolved form and feeds back on dissociation. This is chemically coherent and explains the opposing M0/M2 tendencies.

B. Parallel-response mechanism. Medium and concentration independently control an acid-response channel and a direct precipitation channel, without meaningful causal coupling between them. The present factorial data establish correlation but do not demonstrate feedback.

C. Activity-coefficient or ion-pairing mechanism. The large pH response to concentration could arise primarily from nonideal activities or ion pairing rather than a changing intrinsic K_a. The anonymous benchmark identities may encode these effects categorically.

D. Multiple-acid or latent-buffer mechanism. A second acid/base reservoir whose contribution changes with concentration could explain the pH slope while the reported dissociation fraction tracks only one component.

E. Nucleation/transport mechanism. The possible depression of precipitation at larger scale under high loading could reflect mixing, nucleation statistics, or transport rather than equilibrium solubility.

F. Pure empirical benchmark mapping. Because the environment is a bounded synthetic benchmark, the channels may be generated by coupled latent response functions that admit a chemical analogy but do not correspond uniquely to molecular species. This explanation cannot be excluded and limits claims about real materials.

9. Evidence boundaries and unidentified factors

The following are not identified by this campaign:
- numerical K_a, K_sp, activity coefficients, or solid stoichiometry;
- whether precipitation consumes A-, HA, or another latent species;
- causal direction between dissociation and precipitation;
- kinetic equilibration time, because no waiting-time series was performed;
- temperature dependence, because temperature was not varied;
- catalyst effects, because no catalyst was added;
- behavior outside 0.125-0.500 mol/L or outside 0.040-0.080 L;
- detailed scale effects beyond the single matched pair per entity and concentration;
- physical precipitate mass, morphology, or composition, because precipitation_signal is only a normalized proxy;
- exact M1-versus-M2 ionization ordering near the dissociation detection floor;
- generalization from the categorical benchmark entities to real solvent chemistry.

The small final equilibrium residuals, all no greater than 0.005990, show that the environment classified the final states as internally close to its equilibrium manifold. The reported environment diagnostics ranged from approximately 0.823 to 0.952 and generally increased at high concentration. These are environment diagnostics only; they neither prove thermodynamic equilibrium nor quantify confidence in this report.

10. Supported conclusion

Within the tested benchmark domain, concentration is the dominant transferable control: a fourfold concentration increase lowers pH by about 0.9 unit and increases precipitation in every entity. Entity identity contributes reproducible offsets: M0 is least acidic by pH and least precipitation-prone; M2 is most acidic by pH and most precipitation-prone; M1 is intermediate. The precipitation component of the supplied mapping is well supported. The dissociation component is supported only coarsely because the measured fractions are small, noisy, and frequently at the lower boundary.

A coupled weak-acid/supersaturation model is a useful effective description, but a fixed ideal K_a model is quantitatively insufficient. Medium-dependent activities, nonlinear concentration effects, and either precipitation feedback or a parallel direct-precipitation response are required. The principal concentration and entity relationships transfer approximately across the tested twofold scale change, although a modest high-concentration scale effect on precipitation remains a live alternative.

1. Initial claims: supported, challenged, and untested

The initial material packet contained one substantive task-specific scientific claim: a qualitative selector mapping in which selector 0 had higher acid-ionization tendency and lower solid-formation tendency, selector 1 was intermediate on both, and selector 2 had lower ionization and higher solid formation. It did not provide numerical constants, a complete mechanism, or a material-property dossier. The statement that experimental evidence was authoritative was therefore important: the mapping was a prior to test, not a constraint.

The solid-formation part was supported strongly within the tested domain. In K1 I reported mean final precipitation signals of 0.0212, 0.0369, and 0.0487 for selectors 0, 1, and 2 at 0.125 M, and 0.0564, 0.0716, and 0.1041 at 0.500 M. Both concentration strata independently reproduced selector 0 < selector 1 < selector 2.

The ionization claim received only partial support. At 0.125 M, the mean dissociation fractions followed the prior ordering: 0.0187 for selector 0, 0.00539 for selector 1, and a processed value of zero for selector 2. At 0.500 M, however, selector 1 was reported at zero while selector 2 averaged 0.00376. That is actual counterevidence to the strict selector-1-above-selector-2 ordering, although it is weak counterevidence because the channel noise was comparable to the estimates and several observations were floor-clipped. K1 did revise the claim: it retained only the coarse conclusion that selector 0 appeared more dissociated, while declaring the selector-1 versus selector-2 ordering unidentified. It would be incorrect to describe the high-concentration result merely as an absence of contrary evidence.

The pH observations also created tension with any naive identification of “ionization tendency” with measured acidity. Selector 2 had the lowest pH at both concentrations, despite its nominally lower ionization tendency. This does not directly refute the supplied claim because pH, fractional dissociation, total concentration, activities, and precipitation are not interchangeable. It does refute a simpler interpretation in which one latent ionization parameter alone determines all acid-related observables.

The catalog's warning that selector effects were categorical benchmark couplings, rather than real-solvent predictions, was respected but not experimentally testable inside this world. Likewise, the real names attached to solvent selectors were not evidence that real water, ethanol, or acetonitrile would behave this way.

Untested initial or implicit propositions include transfer beyond 0.125-0.500 M, transfer outside 0.040-0.080 L, temperature and residence-time invariance, catalyst independence, the identity or stoichiometry of the precipitate, and generalization to another world. The campaign found no counterevidence about those propositions because it did not test them; that is not positive support.

2. Experiments that formed or changed the interpretation

Batches 1-4 established the selector-0 baseline. Their matched concentration pairs showed that raising concentration fourfold lowered pH by about 0.88 pH unit and raised precipitation from a mean of 0.0212 to 0.0564. Batches 1 versus 3 and 2 versus 4 also suggested that concentration, rather than total amount or scale, was the primary pH coordinate over the tested twofold volume range.

Batches 5-8 materially changed the explanation. Selector 1 retained a similar concentration-driven pH change but shifted absolute pH downward and precipitation upward relative to selector 0. That was the evidence behind K1's “shared concentration relationship plus entity offsets” description, rather than one universal curve.

Batches 9-12 supplied the strongest entity contrast. Selector 2 had the lowest pH and highest precipitation at both concentrations. Batches 10 and 12, both at 0.500 M but at 0.040 and 0.080 L, gave precipitation signals of 0.10948 and 0.09873. They supported the entity ordering but also raised the possibility of a modest negative scale effect at high concentration. Batch 12 was consequently selected as an evidentiary anchor, not as an optimization winner.

The intermediate/final measurement comparisons changed my assessment of channel reliability. In batch 1, normalized pH changed only from 0.17565 to 0.17396 across the pH meter and final assay, whereas dissociation changed from 0.00466 to 0.02122 and precipitation from 0.00082 to 0.02213. In batch 12, pH changed from 0.09016 to 0.09385, but dissociation changed from 0.01996 to 0.00390 and precipitation from 0.13588 to 0.09873. These observations made pH appear more cross-instrument stable than the other two channels.

The main design choices were made before outcome data were available. Equal coverage of all three selectors followed directly from the entity-mapping goal and the supplied prior. The two concentrations and two scales were an unvalidated but deliberate factorial choice intended to separate concentration from total amount. They also fit the stock limits efficiently. Applying the same pH-meter/final-assay sequence to every batch was a consistency choice rather than an adaptive response. No experiment condition was changed to pursue a favorable result.

Some choices were nevertheless assumptions rather than evidence-based decisions. In particular, 0.125 and 0.500 M were assumed to span an informative response range; 0.040 and 0.080 L were assumed sufficient to test scale transfer; and immediate termination without a residence-time series implicitly assumed that the terminal response was interpretable without first establishing kinetics. Those guesses limited later mechanism identification.

3. Leading competing mechanisms

The most important unresolved competition is between a genuinely coupled acid/precipitation mechanism and two parallel responses driven by common inputs.

In the coupled interpretation, HA dissociates, a dissolved ion or ion pair enters a solubility relation, and precipitation removes a species that feeds back on acid speciation. Effective Ka, activity coefficients, and Ksp all depend on selector identity. This can explain why selector 0 has the clearest fractional dissociation but the weakest precipitation, while selector 2 has strong precipitation and low pH.

In the parallel-response interpretation, selector and concentration independently feed an acid-response function and a direct solid-signal function. Their correlation does not represent chemical feedback. The existing grid cannot distinguish this from true coupling because neither acid speciation nor precipitation was selectively perturbed while holding the other pathway fixed.

A third explanation is concentration-dependent activity or ion pairing without important precipitation feedback. It is favored over a fixed ideal weak-acid law by the magnitude of the pH response. K1 noted that an ideal fixed-Ka model predicts a 0.301-unit pH decrease for a fourfold concentration increase, whereas the observed changes were approximately 0.88-0.95. The simple ideal model is therefore disfavored, but activity effects, a second acid reservoir, latent buffering, and nonlinear benchmark calibration remain mutually confounded.

A fourth explanation is time-dependent nucleation or transport. At high concentration, every larger-volume batch had a lower precipitation signal than its smaller-volume counterpart: differences were approximately -0.00688, -0.01225, and -0.01075 for selectors 0-2. That pattern could be a real mixing or nucleation effect, but there was only one pair per cell and no waiting-time intervention. At low concentration, scale-effect signs were mixed.

Finally, a purely empirical latent benchmark response remains possible. The public contract itself warns against treating the synthetic channels as a real physical instrument or named synthesis. The experiments establish reproducible input-output structure, not unique molecular identities.

The campaign can distinguish robust directional facts—concentration lowers pH and raises precipitation, while selector 2 is more precipitation-prone than selector 0—from the fixed ideal-Ka model. It cannot distinguish coupled feedback from parallel pathways, equilibrium from slowly evolving nucleation, activity effects from a second acid reservoir, or chemical structure from a latent synthetic response function.

4. One additional complete experiment

If exactly one legal complete experiment were allowed, I would repeat the batch-10 composition—selector 2, 0.500 M, 0.040 L—but insert a preregistered 14,400-second wait at a fixed moderate stirring speed before termination. I would take the permitted pH-meter measurement after the wait and then perform the required final assay. I would compare the terminal result with batch 10, which had the same composition and scale without the long wait.

This choice targets the largest unresolved distinction that one experiment can address: stationary equilibrium-like behavior versus time-dependent precipitation or transport. It also uses a condition with a large precipitation signal, avoiding the dissociation floor as much as possible.

Possible interpretations would be:
- If pH, dissociation, and precipitation agree with batch 10 within predictive variability, that would support rapid stationarity and weaken large kinetic or nucleation-delay explanations. It would not by itself distinguish coupled equilibrium from parallel stationary responses.
- If precipitation changes substantially while pH remains stable, I would favor a slow solid-formation, nucleation, or transport process that is at least partly separable from the acid response.
- If precipitation and acid-related channels move together, especially if dissociation and pH shift coherently with precipitation, the coupled-equilibration explanation would gain support.
- If all channels differ erratically, the main lesson would be inadequate repeatability or world/process variability rather than a clean kinetic effect.
- If only dissociation changes while pH remains stable, I would suspect channel-specific measurement sensitivity or latent speciation not captured by pH.

One experiment could not establish a time curve or quantify a rate constant. This proposal is therefore a discriminating probe, not a complete kinetic study.

5. Identifiability versus operational score

The design prioritized mechanism characterization over score maximization. All three selectors received equal coverage, including conditions expected to have low precipitation or lower scalar score. Two concentrations and two scales were retained for every selector rather than concentrating the budget on a favorable region. The intermediate pH measurements consumed the entire nonfinal measurement allowance but supplied cross-instrument and channel-stability information.

This choice followed the research goal, which explicitly asked for entity-conditioned transfer, mapping tests, evidence boundaries, and competing explanations rather than medium ranking or optimization. The native score was also described as a diagnostic rather than the research objective. I did not adapt conditions toward higher equilibrium-confidence diagnostics or precipitation signals after seeing results.

There were costs to that identifiability-first approach. The full factorial used all 12 final assays, leaving no exact same-condition replicates and no time, temperature, or perturbation series. Scale pairs had to serve simultaneously as transfer tests and approximate replicates, so scale effects and random variability could not be separated cleanly. A score-oriented campaign might instead have concentrated on selector 2 at high concentration, where batches 10 and 12 had strong precipitation and high environment diagnostics. That could have improved observed scalar performance while providing much less information about entity contrasts and transfer.

Conversely, the campaign did not maximize mechanistic identifiability either. A stronger identification design would have included residence-time variation or a perturbation intended to separate acid response from solid formation. The balanced grid was broad and interpretable, but shallow. It sacrificed both possible optimization gains and deeper causal intervention in exchange for systematic coverage.

6. Underused evidence and blind-prediction weaknesses

The intermediate measurements were underused. K1 cited batches 1 and 12 as examples but did not systematically model the paired pH-meter/final-assay discrepancies across all 12 batches. Such an analysis could have separated instrument-specific bias from process variation, although it still would not create true biological or process replicates.

The raw signal artifacts, calibration information, replicate pH readings, and final-assay packet structure were also not systematically analyzed in K1. Most conclusions used processed estimates. That was transparent and reproducible at the summary level, but it limited diagnosis of clipping, baseline behavior, and cross-channel covariance. Operational telemetry, the small volume removed by intermediate measurements, and the full pattern of equilibrium residuals were likewise only lightly used.

The scale evidence was difficult to exploit because there were no exact independent replicates. The consistent negative high-concentration precipitation difference across all selectors was noted, but treating it as a real scale law would have overreached. It could equally reflect noise, mixing, or a latent volume-dependent response.

The least reliable blind predictions are Q01-Q03. Their concentration of 0.005 M is 25-fold below the lowest studied concentration, and their volume of 0.024 L is also outside the tested range. K1 explicitly limited support to 0.125-0.500 M and 0.040-0.080 L. The Q01-Q03 pH estimates extrapolated the observed log-concentration slope far beyond that boundary. Their 80% intervals—such as 0.265-0.390 for Q01—may still be too narrow because an ideal weak-acid slope, a low-concentration buffer regime, or a response plateau would yield materially different results.

The Q01-Q03 precipitation predictions are also fragile. Linear extrapolation implied nonzero selector-dependent signals close to zero reagent concentration, but K1 never established whether the precipitation proxy has a physical baseline, a threshold, or a zero-concentration limit. Those model alternatives are not fully represented by the intervals.

Q04-Q06 and Q10-Q12 are less extreme but still extrapolate below 0.125 M. Q04-Q06 additionally use the untested 0.024 L scale. Q10-Q12 are comparatively more reliable because 0.048 L lies within the observed volume range, although their concentration remains outside it. Q07-Q09 extrapolate only modestly from 0.500 to 0.600 M, but the 0.024 L volume and possible nonlinear high-concentration precipitation response remain concerns.

The dissociation predictions throughout Q are particularly uncertain. The prediction rationale used an inverse-square-root concentration heuristic even though K1 had already concluded that a fixed ideal weak-acid model was quantitatively insufficient and that the dissociation channel was often at its floor. This was presented as a heuristic rather than a recovered law, but the resulting intervals—especially Q07-Q09—may be too narrow relative to structural uncertainty. That is a genuine tension with K1's uncertainty statement.

Similarly, K1 called the pH equation an interpolation summary rather than a law outside the grid, whereas Q necessarily extrapolated it. The Q rationales acknowledged the extrapolation and widened intervals, so the inconsistency was disclosed rather than hidden, but disclosure does not ensure adequate coverage. No prediction truth has yet been supplied, so I cannot assess empirical calibration or revise any sealed estimate.

7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation selected batch 12: selector 2, 0.500 M, 0.080 L. Its final result included normalized pH 0.09385, dissociation 0.00390, and precipitation 0.09873. The stated reason was evidentiary: together with batch 10, it completed a matched-concentration scale pair under the strongest precipitation regime.

It was not demonstrated to be optimal. Indeed, batch 10 had a higher observed precipitation signal, 0.10948, at the same concentration and half the volume. The recommendation was not based on a preregistered optimization objective, no local search was performed, and no uncertainty-adjusted comparison of scalar scores was established. Even being the highest observed sample on one metric would not prove optimality; batch 12 was not selected on that basis in any case.

Repeatability should be tested with several independently initialized exact repeats of the batch-12 recipe under a fixed, preregistered protocol. Agreement should be assessed jointly for pH, dissociation, precipitation, missingness, and residuals rather than only for the scalar score. Because batch 12 was selected after observing the campaign, replication should be evaluated as new evidence rather than pooled uncritically with the selection batch.

Local robustness would require small controlled perturbations around 0.500 M and 0.080 L, plus residence-time and mixing perturbations. This would reveal whether the response lies on a broad stable region or near a steep threshold. The existing batch-10 comparison supplies only one coarse volume perturbation and suggests that precipitation may decline at larger scale.

Cross-material transfer would require repeating the same concentration-scale protocol for other selectors with actual replicates. The campaign contains selector contrasts, but only one batch per selector-scale-concentration cell, so it cannot separate material effects from cell-level variability with high precision.

Cross-world generalization is even less established. The material contract defines categorical synthetic benchmark effects, and no second world, latent parameterization, or real-material system was tested. Demonstrating transfer would require preregistered repetition across independently instantiated worlds or external material systems using the same observables and decision rule.

The proper conclusion is therefore that batch 12 is a useful observed anchor for one local benchmark regime. It is neither a proven optimum nor a generally robust operating recommendation.

predictions.rationale: This is a large downward concentration extrapolation for selector 0. I extrapolated the observed log-concentration pH relationship, allowed fractional dissociation to increase approximately as inverse square root concentration, and widened all intervals substantially.

The selector-1 offsets were applied to the same low-concentration extrapolation. Dissociation is poorly identified near its measurement floor, so its interval includes zero and is deliberately asymmetric.
Selector 2 is predicted to retain the lowest pH and greatest precipitation among the three entities. The concentration is far outside the observed range, making functional-form uncertainty dominant.

The 0.08 M condition is a modest extrapolation below the observed 0.125 M boundary. The 0.024 L scale is also below the studied range, so the interval includes extra scale uncertainty despite the previously small pH scale effects.

This applies the selector-1 entity offsets and the shared concentration response. The dissociation estimate remains close to the assay floor, while precipitation is expected to be intermediate between selectors 0 and 2.
The prediction preserves the experimentally repeated selector ordering in pH and precipitation. Dissociation for selector 2 was not cleanly resolved, so its interval includes the lower boundary.

The concentration is only modestly above the observed 0.5 M condition. I extended the log-concentration pH trend and local precipitation slope while allowing for nonlinear high-concentration behavior and the smaller untested volume.

Selector 1 is predicted to remain intermediate in pH and precipitation at 0.6 M. Its dissociation channel was frequently at the processed floor, producing a broad bounded interval relative to the point estimate.

Selector 2 had the strongest observed precipitation response and lowest pH at both studied concentrations. The precipitation interval is wider because its concentration response appeared steeper than for selectors 0 and 1.
This shares the Q04 concentration and entity prediction, but 0.048 L lies within the experimentally bracketed scale range. The intervals are therefore narrower than for the 0.024 L counterpart.

The matched-concentration scale results suggested approximate transfer across volume, especially for pH. I therefore retained the selector-1 point predictions and used uncertainty dominated by concentration extrapolation and assay variability.

The selector-2 entity effects are carried over at the in-range 0.048 L scale. The prediction maintains higher precipitation and lower pH than the other selectors while acknowledging weak identification of dissociation.

payload.rationale: Predictions use the completed 12-batch campaign only. Normalized pH was modeled with a shared approximately linear dependence on log concentration plus entity offsets, because the observed fourfold concentration change produced similar pH shifts for all selectors. Precipitation was locally extrapolated from each selector's concentration slope while preserving the robust selector-0 < selector-1 < selector-2 ordering. Dissociation was treated as a weak-acid-like, approximately inverse-square-root concentration response, but with strong shrinkage and wide bounded intervals because many training values were comparable to assay noise or reported at zero. Scale was treated as a secondary effect: predictions at 0.048 L receive narrower intervals because that volume lies within the studied 0.040-0.080 L range, whereas 0.024 L predictions include additional uncertainty. All intervals are predictive 80% intervals, incorporate instrument variability and model-form uncertainty, and are clipped to the public metric range [0,1].

evidentiary_anchor.selection_rationale: Batch 12 is a useful evidentiary anchor because its high-loading, large-scale medium-2 condition completes a matched-concentration scale pair with batch 10 and shows clearly resolved pH and precipitation responses.

payload.report:
Mechanistic report

1. Experimental scope and design

I completed 12 ambient-condition batches spanning three selectable medium identities, denoted M0, M1, and M2. For each medium I tested nominal reagent concentrations of 0.10, 0.25, and 0.40 mol/L. The 0.10 mol/L condition was run at both 0.03 L and 0.06 L, giving one scale-transfer pair per medium. Each batch received an intermediate pH-meter measurement and a post-termination final assay. No catalyst, heating, time course, or deliberate equilibration-time variation was tested.

The concentration/scale assignments were:
- M0: batches 1–4
- M1: batches 5–8
- M2: batches 9–12
- Within each group: 0.10 mol/L at 0.03 L, 0.10 mol/L at 0.06 L, 0.25 mol/L at 0.06 L, and 0.40 mol/L at 0.06 L.

I treat the final assay as the principal quantitative evidence because its declared noise is lower than that of the intermediate pH meter for the response variables of interest. Intermediate measurements are useful as consistency checks but are not additional concentration or scale conditions.

2. Principal observations

The final-assay results were:

Batch | Medium | C (mol/L) | Volume (L) | pH normalized | pH (=14×normalized) | Dissociation fraction | Precipitation signal
1 | M0 | 0.10 | 0.03 | 0.18794 | 2.631 | 0.00599 | 0.01071
2 | M0 | 0.10 | 0.06 | 0.18010 | 2.521 | 0.01877 | 0.01121
3 | M0 | 0.25 | 0.06 | 0.14262 | 1.997 | 0.00841 | 0.04395

12 | M2 | 0.40 | 0.06 | 0.10258 | 1.436 | 0.00000 | 0.08722

The strongest reproducible structures are:

(a) Increasing concentration lowers pH in every medium. From the mean 0.10 mol/L result to 0.40 mol/L, normalized pH fell from 0.1840 to 0.1227 for M0, from 0.1793 to 0.1087 for M1, and from 0.1714 to 0.1026 for M2.

(b) Increasing concentration raises the precipitation proxy in every medium. The corresponding changes were approximately 0.0110 to 0.0463 for M0, 0.0216 to 0.0674 for M1, and 0.0369 to 0.0872 for M2.

(c) The medium effect is ordered and largely transfers across concentration: M2 generally gives the lowest pH and largest precipitation signal, M1 is intermediate, and M0 gives the smallest precipitation signal and usually the highest pH. At 0.25 mol/L, for example, precipitation was 0.04395, 0.05982, and 0.07533 for M0, M1, and M2, respectively. At 0.40 mol/L it was 0.04629, 0.06744, and 0.08722.

(d) The reported dissociation fraction is very small, often at its zero boundary, and does not show a stable monotonic concentration trend. Its medium-wide means were approximately 0.00862 for M0, 0.00359 for M1, and 0.00193 for M2, but these averages are dominated by a few small positive readings, especially batch 2. I therefore do not regard this channel alone as a reliable estimate of a conventional thermodynamic degree of dissociation.

3. Empirical relationships

A compact descriptive response surface over the tested range is

pH_norm(C,M) ≈ a_M + b_M log10(C / 1 mol L^-1).

Least-squares fits to the four final-assay observations per medium gave:
- M0: a=0.08160, b=-0.10232
- M1: a=0.06350, b=-0.11611
- M2: a=0.05678, b=-0.11461

Thus concentration dependence is similar for M1 and M2 and somewhat shallower for M0. In ordinary pH units, the fitted slopes are about -1.43, -1.63, and -1.60 pH units per decade of concentration. These slopes are much steeper than the ideal -0.5 pH-unit-per-decade dependence of an isolated dilute monoprotic weak acid under the simplest approximation. That discrepancy is evidence that a one-equilibrium ideal weak-acid equation is inadequate here; activity effects, precipitation coupling, a direct medium response, or a combination of these is required. The fitted intercepts are mathematical parameters and should not be interpreted as measured responses at 1 mol/L.

A simple linear description of the precipitation proxy over 0.10–0.40 mol/L is

P(C,M) ≈ q_M + s_M C,

with:
- M0: q=0.00104, s=0.1270 L/mol
- M1: q=0.00823, s=0.1619 L/mol
- M2: q=0.02168, s=0.1759 L/mol

This expresses two observed medium effects: an increasing baseline offset from M0 to M2 and a modest increase in concentration sensitivity. It is only a local empirical approximation. A precipitation proxy must eventually be nonlinear, thresholded, or bounded, so neither negative-concentration nor high-concentration extrapolation of these lines is justified.

4. Proposed process interpretation

My minimal mechanistic picture is a coupled acid-ionization and solid-removal system:

HA ⇌ H+ + A−

K_a,eff(M) = a(H+)a(A−)/a(HA),

followed by a medium-dependent solid-forming process involving an ionized or associated solution species:

νA− + X ⇌ Solid,

with precipitation becoming appreciable when an effective ion product exceeds a medium-dependent threshold. A schematic mass balance is

C_total = [HA] + [A−] + νS,

where S is the amount transferred to solid or to whatever latent state generates the bounded precipitation signal.

The medium can act through at least three latent functions:
1. acid activities and therefore K_a,eff or the relationship between hydrogen activity and analytical concentration;
2. the solid-formation threshold or effective solubility product;
3. the mapping between actual solid amount or morphology and the normalized precipitation sensor.

Precipitation and dissociation are coupled because removing an ionized or associated species can shift the acid equilibrium. Conversely, pH controls the population of ionized precursor available for solid formation. The data establish that both outputs respond to concentration and medium, but they do not identify the direction or stoichiometry of the microscopic coupling.

The combination of lower pH and greater precipitation in M2 can be explained by a medium that independently favors hydrogen activity and solid formation. It could also arise from a single coupled process in which increased ionization supplies more precipitating precursor and precipitation then pulls further dissociation. The near-zero measured dissociation fractions prevent discrimination between these versions.

5. Scale transfer

At 0.10 mol/L, changing volume from 0.03 to 0.06 L changed normalized pH by:
- M0: -0.00783
- M1: +0.00235
- M2: -0.00131

The corresponding precipitation-signal changes were:
- M0: +0.00050
- M1: +0.00149
- M2: -0.00781

These contrasts are small relative to the concentration and medium effects, except for the M0 pH difference and possibly the M2 precipitation difference. This supports approximate concentration-based transfer across a twofold scale change, but only weakly: there was one batch at each scale, so run variability and scale effects cannot be separated. Batch 1 versus batch 2 also produced dissociation fractions of 0.00599 and 0.01877, demonstrating that this small-valued channel is not reproducibly scale-invariant at the available precision.

6. How the evidence changed the qualitative prior

The supplied qualitative mapping proposed intermediate acid ionization and solid formation for M0, lower ionization and higher solid formation for M1, and higher ionization and lower solid formation for M2.

The pH evidence partly supports the claim that M2 has the strongest effective acidic response: M2 had the lowest pH at every matched condition. It does not support the complete stated ionization ordering. M1 was not consistently less acidic than M0; at 0.25 and 0.40 mol/L its pH was lower than M0, while the 0.10 mol/L scale pair was nearly tied. The direct dissociation-fraction channel is too close to zero and too variable to settle this issue.

The proposed solid-formation ordering is contradicted by all matched final-assay comparisons. The observed order was M2 > M1 > M0, whereas the prior implied M1 > M0 > M2. This reversal occurred at both scales at 0.10 mol/L and at 0.25 and 0.40 mol/L. I therefore revise the local empirical entity map to: M2 has the largest precipitation response, M1 is intermediate, and M0 is lowest within the tested domain.

Batch 7 was selected as the final evidentiary anchor. It is the central 0.25 mol/L M1 condition, with normalized pH 0.13496, dissociation fraction 0.00727, and precipitation signal 0.05982. It is bracketed by lower- and higher-concentration M1 batches and has corresponding M0 and M2 comparisons, while none of its principal channels sits exactly at a zero boundary.

7. Measurement consistency and diagnostics

Intermediate and final measurements agreed well on pH but were sometimes quite different for the small dissociation and precipitation channels. For example, batch 1 gave intermediate versus final dissociation fractions of 0.03336 and 0.00599; batch 2 gave 0 and 0.01877. Batch 10 gave intermediate versus final precipitation signals of 0.07437 and 0.03295. This is consistent with the larger declared noise of the intermediate instrument, possible clipping at zero, and possibly different measurement timing. It is not evidence by itself for chemical evolution because timing and instrument identity were not independently varied.

Final-assay equilibrium residuals ranged from 0 to 0.00696. The environment diagnostic named equilibrium_confidence ranged approximately from 0.846 to 0.960. I use those values only as environment or fit diagnostics, not as my scientific confidence and not as proof that a unique thermodynamic equilibrium mechanism has been identified.

8. Evidence boundaries and competing explanations

Supported within the experiment domain:
- Concentration is the dominant continuous control variable for pH and precipitation.
- Medium identity shifts both response surfaces.
- The local precipitation ordering is M2 > M1 > M0.
- Concentration-based behavior approximately transfers from 0.03 to 0.06 L at 0.10 mol/L.
- A simple isolated ideal weak-acid model is insufficient to describe the observed concentration dependence.

Not identified:
- A numerical thermodynamic K_a or K_sp.
- Activity coefficients, solid stoichiometry, nucleation mechanism, crystal identity, or true precipitated mass.
- Whether the medium acts on equilibrium thermodynamics, kinetics, sensor response, or several of these.
- Equilibration time, reversibility, hysteresis, or whether precipitation is nucleation-limited.
- Temperature dependence, catalyst effects, behavior beyond 0.10–0.40 mol/L, or scale behavior beyond 0.03–0.06 L.
- A reliable law for the reported dissociation-fraction channel near its zero boundary.

Reasonable competing explanations include:
1. Independent medium effects: one latent parameter controls hydrogen activity while another controls solid formation.
2. A genuinely coupled equilibrium in which precipitation removes an ionized species and shifts acid dissociation.
3. Kinetic or nucleation effects masquerading as equilibrium differences because only one terminal time was sampled.
4. Medium-dependent activity coefficients causing pH shifts without large changes in true molecular dissociation.
5. A medium-dependent mapping from solid amount or morphology to the normalized precipitation proxy.
6. Censoring and noise in the near-zero dissociation channel, which could conceal a weak but systematic trend.

Finally, the selectable media are benchmark identities with categorical runtime effects. These observations should not be generalized into claims about real water, ethanol, or acetonitrile chemistry. The defensible conclusion is a bounded empirical mechanism for this synthetic weak-acid/direct-precipitation world, not a universal aqueous-chemistry law.

1. Assessment of the initial claims

The initial material packet did contain one substantive task-specific prior: M0 was described as intermediate in acid ionization and solid formation, M1 as lower in ionization and higher in solid formation, and M2 as higher in ionization and lower in solid formation. It was explicitly a qualitative local mapping rather than a complete mechanism.

The acidic-response part received mixed support. At every matched condition, M2 had the lowest final pH, which supports the claim that it produces the strongest effective acidic response. For example, at 0.25 mol/L the normalized pH values in batches 3, 7, and 11 were 0.14262, 0.13496, and 0.12549 for M0, M1, and M2. However, the measured dissociation fraction did not support the same ordering: its medium-wide final-assay means decreased from M0 to M2, and several M2 observations were at zero. Thus there was genuine counterevidence in one measurement channel, not merely an absence of confirmation. K1 acknowledged that conflict but favored the reproducible pH ordering and treated the dissociation channel as boundary-censored and unreliable. That was defensible, although it means the claimed microscopic ionization ordering remained unresolved rather than demonstrated.

The proposed solid-formation ordering was directly contradicted. The observed precipitation order was M2 > M1 > M0 at every matched concentration and scale. At 0.40 mol/L, batches 4, 8, and 12 produced 0.04629, 0.06744, and 0.08722, respectively, whereas the prior implied M1 > M0 > M2. K1 explicitly revised this mapping; this was not counterevidence that went unnoticed or remained uncorrected.

Other statements in the packet—such as describing the task as a bounded weak-acid/direct-precipitation slice—defined the synthetic world and its observable channels. The experiments were consistent with concentration-dependent acidity and a precipitation proxy, but they did not independently prove that the underlying microscopic process was direct precipitation, establish a solid identity, or validate a physical aqueous mechanism. Likewise, the synthetic-instrument calibration and boundary statements were contractual information, not hypotheses tested by the campaign.

2. Experiments that formed or changed the interpretation

The design itself was mostly fixed before useful outcome data existed. I chose a balanced matrix of three selectors, three concentrations, and one twofold scale contrast per selector because the research goal emphasized entity mapping, concentration transfer, and scale transfer. The choice of 0.10, 0.25, and 0.40 mol/L and the assumption that a twofold volume change would be informative were design judgments, not results established by the initial packet. The qualitative prior justified covering all three selectors but did not determine these numerical conditions.

The first decisive evidence against the solid-formation prior came from the matched 0.10 mol/L conditions. Batches 1, 5, and 9 at 0.03 L gave precipitation signals of 0.01071, 0.02090, and 0.04076. Batches 2, 6, and 10 at 0.06 L gave 0.01121, 0.02238, and 0.03295. By the completion of batch 10, the prior ordering had already been contradicted at both scales. I did not change the remaining experimental matrix because it had been fixed in advance; that was preservation of design rather than failure to notice the evidence.

The most influential confirmation came from the concentration-matched triples at 0.25 mol/L and 0.40 mol/L. Batches 3, 7, and 11 established the M0 < M1 < M2 precipitation order at an interior concentration, while batches 4, 8, and 12 showed that it persisted at the high end of the sampled range. Those same triples established the inverse pH ordering. Their agreement caused me to interpret the selector effect as transferable across concentration rather than as an isolated low-concentration anomaly.

The paired scale observations shaped the narrower claim of approximate—not exact—scale transfer. Batches 5 and 6 were especially consistent, while batches 1 and 2 differed in normalized pH by 0.00783 and batches 9 and 10 differed in precipitation by 0.00781. Those discrepancies prevented a claim of strict scale invariance.

The erratic dissociation results changed my confidence in that channel. Examples include batch 1, whose intermediate and final dissociation estimates were 0.03336 and 0.00599, and batch 2, whose estimates were 0 and 0.01877. Those disagreements led K1 to avoid fitting a precise dissociation law.

One important design weakness is that I ran all M0 batches first, then all M1 batches, then all M2 batches. Consequently, selector is confounded with campaign order. The consistency across concentration and scale is useful, but randomizing or interleaving selectors would have provided stronger protection against drift or order effects.

3. Main competing mechanisms and what can be distinguished

The leading interpretations remain:

(a) Independent medium effects: selector identity separately changes hydrogen activity and the propensity or sensor response for solid formation.

(b) Coupled equilibrium: ionization generates a precipitating precursor, precipitation removes that precursor, and removal shifts the acid equilibrium.

(c) Kinetic or nucleation control: the terminal response reflects selector-dependent rates or induction times rather than only equilibrium constants.

(d) Activity-coefficient effects: pH changes substantially even if the molecular dissociation fraction changes little.

(e) Observation-model effects: selector-dependent solid morphology or matrix response changes the normalized precipitation signal without a proportional change in solid amount.

The experiments distinguish a simple ideal, isolated weak-acid model from a more complex response. In K1, the fitted normalized-pH slopes were approximately -0.102 to -0.116 per concentration decade, equivalent to about -1.43 to -1.63 ordinary pH units per decade. That is much steeper than the simplest ideal weak-acid approximation. The experiments also robustly distinguish the local empirical selector order and demonstrate strong concentration dependence.

They do not distinguish independent medium effects from genuine acid–precipitation coupling. No intervention changed precipitation while holding the acidic environment fixed, or vice versa. They also do not separate equilibrium from kinetics because there was no deliberate time series, waiting-time contrast, or reversibility test. The precipitation observable was a bounded proxy rather than a gravimetric solid measurement, so thermodynamic solubility, nucleation, morphology, and sensor response remain aliased. The near-zero dissociation channel further prevents reliable estimation of Ka-like parameters or coupling stoichiometry.

4. One additional complete experiment

If allowed exactly one additional legal experiment, I would repeat the batch-11 composition—M2, 0.25 mol/L, 0.06 L—but introduce a long, controlled stirred wait before termination and final assay. I would use the available intermediate pH measurement after the wait rather than immediately after mixing. Batch 11 supplies the closest no-deliberate-wait comparator and has a substantial precipitation signal without being at the highest tested concentration.

Possible interpretations would be:

- If pH and precipitation remained close to batch 11 (final normalized pH 0.12549 and precipitation 0.07533), it would support rapid establishment and local temporal stability. It would weaken, but not eliminate, a slow nucleation or equilibration explanation.
- If precipitation increased materially while pH shifted in the direction predicted by additional ionization, that would support a time-dependent coupled-removal process.
- If precipitation changed materially but pH did not, independent nucleation, morphology, or sensor-response kinetics would become more plausible.
- If pH changed but precipitation did not, slow acid/activity equilibration independent of solid formation would become more plausible.
- If both signals moved irregularly or the result merely differed within existing run variability, the experiment would be inconclusive and would demonstrate the need for replication rather than justify a new mechanism.

A single waited batch could not establish a kinetic law, because it would still lack replicate runs and multiple time points. Its purpose would be to target the largest current mechanistic ambiguity, not to complete the identification.

5. Trade-off between mechanistic identifiability and operational score

The campaign prioritized characterization over score optimization. I spent all 12 complete experiments on a balanced selector/concentration/scale matrix rather than repeatedly running whichever condition appeared to have the most favorable scalar diagnostic. This directly followed the research goal, which explicitly concerned entity mapping and transfer rather than medium ranking or optimization.

The scale pairs consumed three batches that could instead have extended the concentration range or replicated apparent high-score conditions. That was a deliberate sacrifice of potential optimization breadth for a limited test of scale transfer. Likewise, sampling all three selectors at unfavorable as well as favorable conditions improved identifiability but was not an efficient strategy for maximizing a single score.

Conversely, the design did not maximize mechanistic identifiability in every respect. It omitted time, temperature, catalyst, reversibility, and randomized order. Those omissions kept the matrix feasible and preserved full selector/concentration coverage, but they left major mechanisms aliased. The concentration grid also provided only one observation at 0.25 and 0.40 mol/L per selector, so response curvature and stochastic variation could not be separated.

There is no evidence that I knowingly sacrificed identifiability to chase a high score. The environment diagnostic named equilibrium_confidence was reported but not treated as the scientific objective. Nor did I select batch 7 because it maximized that diagnostic: batch 12 had a higher value. Batch 7 was chosen as an interior evidentiary anchor with resolved channels and matched comparisons.

6. Underused evidence and weaknesses in the blind predictions

The processed final-assay values were used much more fully than the raw evidence. The raw spectral peaks, channel assignments, mass-balance fields, electrode signals, and replicate pH values were not modeled quantitatively. Some of those fields might have helped diagnose clipping, matrix response, or measurement inconsistency, although the public packet did not provide enough empirical calibration to convert them into independent species concentrations. Operational telemetry was also largely unused because temperature and pressure were not intentionally varied.

The intermediate measurements were difficult to exploit. They differed from the final assay in both instrument noise and timing, so a disagreement could represent noise, termination-associated evolution, or a channel-specific calibration effect. K1 noted examples but did not construct a formal cross-instrument error model. The sequence-wide order confound was also not incorporated quantitatively into the final uncertainty.

The least reliable blind predictions are Q01–Q03 at 0.005 mol/L. They extrapolate twentyfold below the lowest experimental concentration. K1 explicitly said that the empirical pH and precipitation fits were local to 0.10–0.40 mol/L and that low-concentration threshold behavior was unidentified. The prediction rationale acknowledged the extrapolation, but the numerical pH intervals—roughly 0.26–0.39—may still be too narrow because the fitted log-concentration slope could flatten substantially below 0.10 mol/L. The dissociation predictions are even less secure because they impose dilution-driven increases on a channel for which K1 declined to identify a reliable law.

Q07–Q09 at 0.60 mol/L are the next most vulnerable. The extrapolation is shorter, but the precipitation predictions extend local linear fits even though K1 warned that the bounded proxy must eventually curve or saturate. Their upper and lower bounds may be too narrow if a threshold, saturation, or new solid regime occurs above 0.40 mol/L.

Q04–Q06 and Q10–Q12 are closer to the observed domain, but the paired scale predictions may also be overconfident. I assigned identical point estimates at 0.024 and 0.048 L and represented scale uncertainty mainly through interval width. That is consistent with K1's statement of approximate scale transfer, but the M0 pH and M2 precipitation scale discrepancies, lack of replication, and different requested volumes make exact equality an assumption rather than an observed law.

Thus the prediction text was qualitatively consistent with K1's stated boundaries, but some numerical intervals did not fully propagate the degree of model-form uncertainty expressed in K1. No prediction truth has been supplied, so these are prospective self-criticisms, not post hoc explanations of prediction errors.

7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation selected batch 7: M1 at 0.25 mol/L and 0.06 L, with normalized pH 0.13496, dissociation fraction 0.00727, and precipitation signal 0.05982. Its rationale was evidentiary: it was an interior condition, was bracketed by lower and higher concentrations, had direct M0 and M2 comparators, and none of its principal final channels was exactly at zero.

It was not proven repeatable. There was only one batch at that exact selector, concentration, and volume. It was also not demonstrated to be locally robust because neighboring concentrations were relatively distant and no small perturbations in amount, volume, timing, or temperature were tested.

A proper repeatability test would run multiple exact batch-7 replicates, randomized among other selectors to remove campaign-order confounding, and report all failures and between-run dispersion. Local robustness would require nearby concentrations such as 0.20 and 0.30 mol/L, modest volume changes at fixed concentration, and at least one waiting-time perturbation. Cross-material generalization would require applying the same design to other selector identities under the same observation contract. Cross-world generalization would require independent worlds or parameterizations, because the material packet explicitly described categorical benchmark effects rather than universal solvent chemistry.

Finally, batch 7 was not claimed to be the sample-in highest-scoring condition, and the evidence does not establish that it was. Even a sample-in maximum would only be the largest observed value among 12 noisy, sparsely sampled batches; it would not prove global or local optimality. The sealed selection should therefore be read as a well-connected characterization anchor, not as an optimized operating recommendation.

M2 is predicted to remain the most acidic and precipitation-prone entity, but 0.005 mol/L lies far outside the measured concentration range. The interval allows substantial curvature or a low-concentration precipitation threshold.
This is a short extrapolation from the two M0 observations at 0.10 mol/L. The prediction mainly uses concentration rather than total amount because the observed twofold scale contrast was small.
The estimate extends the local M1 response slightly below 0.10 mol/L. It retains the observed intermediate entity effect and includes uncertainty from the near-zero dissociation channel.
The M2 estimate preserves its lower-pH, higher-precipitation ordering. Uncertainty is wider for precipitation because the two measured M2 scale replicates differed more than those of M0 and M1.
This modest high-concentration extrapolation extends the M0 log-pH and local linear precipitation trends beyond 0.40 mol/L. The interval allows precipitation nonlinearity and bounded-channel effects.
